intro: Venera 13 landed on Venus on 1 March 1982, just east of Phoebe Regio, and kept working for 127 minutes in 457 °C heat under about 90 times the air pressure at sea level on Earth — four times its 32-minute design life. It sent the first colour pictures of the Venusian surface and drilled a sample of the ground, which its X-ray instrument found to be a potassium-rich basalt.

images.caption: A labelled model of a Venera spacecraft of this generation: the carrier with its engine, solar panels and dish antenna, and on top the sphere that carried the lander down.
The 1982 Soviet stamp for Venera 13 and its twin Venera 14, which landed four days later about 950 km away.
A black-and-white frame from Venera 13: flat slabs of rock and dark soil, with the lander's own hardware along the edge. The camera looked out through a window and swept from side to side.
The colour panorama, reprocessed: the first colour view of the ground on Venus. The lander's own saw-toothed ring runs along the bottom of both halves.
